Introduction/Concepts

Development guide

Concepts

Use these concepts to make AI-assisted development easier to direct and review. Each section explains a practical problem, a way to address it and a small example.

An AI agent uses a model to choose or adapt actions and tool use towards a goal, within agreed permissions and limits. A workflow can combine agents with predefined code paths and automated checks. The concepts below explain how to define the task, support the agent and review its work. [9]

These are related practices, not lifecycle stages. Start with the relationship map, then follow the reading route or choose the concept that addresses your current problem.

On this page
How the concepts fit together Intent-driven development Spec-driven development Context engineering Harness engineering Loop engineering Graph engineering Software factories AI models Sources and learning references

How the concepts fit together

These are the working definitions used in this guide. Usage overlaps across authors and tools. Here, graph engineering refers to execution and workflow graphs rather than knowledge graphs.

The concepts address different parts of the same work. Intent-driven development explains why a change is needed. Spec-driven development defines what the software should do and how the team will check it.

Context engineering supplies the information an AI agent needs. Harness engineering provides its tools, permissions and checks. Loop engineering defines how it responds to feedback; graph engineering organises steps and dependencies. A software factory brings these practices into a delivery workflow.

For example, a team wants users to resume an unfinished service request. The team agrees the goal, writes acceptance criteria, gives the agent the relevant information and tools, and reviews the result. Model selection supports that work.

Relationship map: the question each concept helps answer
ConceptQuestion
IntentWhy is the change needed, and which outcomes and constraints matter?
SpecificationWhat behaviour is required, and how will the team check it?
ContextWhich information does the agent need for this task?
HarnessWhich tools, permissions and checks let the agent act within agreed limits?
Feedback loopsHow does feedback guide another attempt, a change of approach or a stop?
Workflow dependenciesWhich agent tasks can run in parallel, and how do decision points join and route findings?
Software factoryHow do these practices connect agreed work to review, release and support?
Model selectionWhich model meets this task’s quality, time, cost and data-handling needs?

The relationships also work in reverse: a failed check may reveal missing context or an unclear requirement. Use the finding to revisit the relevant practice. The examples below use a fictional service-request application to show how these practices work together.

Intent-driven development

Intent-driven development means agreeing why a change is needed before choosing a solution. Record the user’s problem, the intended outcome and the limits the solution needs to respect.

Use it when a request leaves room for conflicting interpretations. “Improve the form” could mean a new layout, fewer questions or a way to save unfinished work. Agree the user need before asking an agent to implement a solution.

Agree the outcome and constraints

  • Problem: who is affected, and what prevents them from completing their task?
  • Outcome: what should the user be able to do after the change?
  • Constraints: which access rules, data-handling requirements or existing behaviours need to remain?
  • Open questions: what is undecided, who will resolve it and when is the decision needed?

Example · Help users continue an unfinished request

A product owner asks an AI agent to “improve the request form”. Before the agent changes it, the team agrees what needs to improve:

  • Problem: users leave the form to find missing information. When they return, their entries are gone and they have to start again.
  • Outcome: users can leave an unfinished request and return later to continue from where they stopped.
  • Constraints: only the request’s owner can reopen it. Keeping unfinished work must not submit the request or notify a reviewer.
  • Open question: should progress be saved automatically or when the user selects “Save draft”? The product owner will decide after testing both options with users.

The agent uses this intent to propose and prototype the two options. Users try leaving and reopening a request; the team checks whether they can continue without re-entering information.

The product owner uses those findings to choose how saving should work. The team then writes the detailed acceptance criteria for implementation.

Keep the record proportionate

A short issue may be enough for a small defect. A new capability may need research and a product requirements document. Recording a goal does not establish that it is valuable; test important assumptions before committing substantial effort.

Next step: Write the problem, outcome and constraints for one change. Then use the product thesis guidance to test the case for it, or define its acceptance criteria when the need is understood.

Source: [1].

Spec-driven development

Specification-driven development, or spec-driven development, uses written requirements to guide development and review. The specification describes the expected behaviour, including important exceptions and constraints. Acceptance criteria state how the team will judge whether that behaviour works.

Use it when a broad request leaves developers or agents to guess the details. “Saving works” does not explain what happens when a connection fails, another user requests the draft or two browser tabs make changes.

Use the requirements to guide both development and testing

Before development, the specification informs the technical design and tasks. During review, tests and reviewers compare the working software with the same acceptance criteria. Keep design choices in the technical plan so developers can choose how to meet the requirements.

Example · Describe what “Save draft” means

The team chooses an explicit “Save draft” action. It agrees these acceptance criteria before implementation:

  • Incomplete form: saving keeps the entered values without submitting the request.
  • Successful save: show “Draft saved” after the server confirms it. Reopening the draft restores the saved values.
  • Failed save: retain the values on screen, explain the failure and offer a retry.
  • Access control: reject another user’s attempt to read or change the draft, including requests made outside the browser interface.
  • Conflicting edits: if another browser tab has saved a newer version, explain the conflict and preserve the unsaved values.

Add detail as decisions become clearer

Too little detail forces the team to invent product rules. Too much detail before research can make an untested idea look settled. Resolve important unknowns, then update the specification as the team learns. Human review still covers judgements that automated tests cannot settle.

Next step: Check one requirement for its success, failure and access-control cases. Use the requirements handover checklist, then translate it into technical design and development tasks.

Source: [2].

Context engineering

Context engineering means selecting and maintaining the information an AI agent needs for its current task. That information can include requirements, relevant code, team standards, test results and earlier decisions.

Use it when an agent follows an outdated rule, misses a business meaning or cannot find a decision. Supplying more documents alone does not solve the problem. Give the agent the relevant information and a clear way to find further detail.

Choose relevant, current and authoritative sources

Start with the task’s goal, acceptance criteria and constraints. Add the code and standards needed for the change. Confirm the applicable source with its owner when documents disagree. Record important decisions where the next person or agent can find them.

Example · Filter service requests by status

An agent is asked to add an “Open requests” filter. The label alone does not explain which statuses count as open or which records the user may see.

The developer supplies the current product decision and the code that implements request search:

  • Product rule: “Open” includes submitted and in-progress requests; drafts and closed requests are excluded.
  • Interface behaviour: the selected filter appears in the URL so refreshing preserves it.
  • API contract: the search endpoint accepts the corresponding status values and applies the user’s access restrictions.
  • Application code: the existing filter component, status definitions, search handler and related tests.

The agent implements the filter using those definitions. The developer checks the returned records, refresh behaviour and access restrictions against the agreed examples.

If an older document includes drafts in “Open”, the developer resolves the conflict with the product owner and records the applicable decision before implementation continues.

Keep decisions available beyond the conversation

Save decisions, unresolved questions and progress in the repository or issue tracker. A future session needs access to those records to use them. Keep source versions where they affect the decision, and follow the applicable data-handling rules.

Relevant information improves the basis for the work; it does not guarantee a correct result. Review retrieved material before relying on it. A document or log does not gain authority merely because an agent found it.

Next step: List the information missing from one recent task. Use the context-by-stage guide to identify the right source, then prepare and check that source.

Source: [3].

Harness engineering

Harness engineering means designing the tools, permissions, checks and progress records around an AI agent. This supporting environment is the agent’s harness. It lets the agent do the work, observe the result and stay within agreed limits.

Use it when an agent cannot run the application, check a result or resume unfinished work. A better prompt cannot replace a missing test environment or an access control.

Provide the tools and controls the task needs

The six components below are one way to describe the supporting environment. They work together rather than running as six consecutive steps.

  • Agent state: what the agent is doing now and what it will try next.
  • Tools: the actions it can perform, such as reading files, using a browser or running tests.
  • Memory: saved decisions, progress and reference information that later work can retrieve.
  • Orchestration: how tasks are assigned, ordered and handed over.
  • Safety: permissions, allowed actions and limits on time, attempts or spending.
  • Observability: records of actions and results that help people investigate and review the work.

Example · Equip a coding agent to build file uploads

A developer asks a coding agent to add attachments to a request form. Users need to upload a file and reopen it later.

Before the agent starts, the developer configures its harness:

  • Agent state: a task checklist tracks whether the agent is inspecting the code, implementing the change or checking the result.
  • Tools: a code editor, terminal and browser let the agent change files, start the application and run tests. A test account, sample files and local storage support upload checks.
  • Memory: repository instructions and saved progress notes keep setup commands, decisions and unfinished work available when the agent resumes.
  • Orchestration: the workflow directs the agent through implementation and checks, then hands the changes and results to the developer for review.
  • Safety: workspace permissions allow changes to the project and test storage. The environment blocks access to production credentials and deployment tools.
  • Observability: the harness records changed files, commands, test results and browser screenshots so the developer can inspect what happened.

The agent edits the upload code, adds tests and runs the application. It uses the browser to upload a sample file and reopen the saved attachment.

If local storage is unavailable, the agent records the failed check and stops for help. Otherwise, it returns the changes and test results for the developer to review before merging.

Check the environment as well as the output

Provide a repeatable way to start the application, run tests and inspect failures. Enforce permissions through the tools and execution environment. Keep a reviewer responsible for acceptance; an agent’s assessment of its own work is not independent review.

When failures recur, inspect the instructions, sources, tools and checks before adding more retries or access. Maintain the harness as the application changes.

Next step: Check whether a developer can start the application, run its tests and inspect a failure using the documented setup. Follow the Eitri installation guide and team setup checklist to fill the gaps.

Sources: [4]; [5]; [6].

Loop engineering

Loop engineering means designing how an agent uses feedback to improve its work over several attempts. A feedback loop connects an action, an observed result and a decision to continue, change approach or stop. Across tasks, review findings and evaluations can also guide updates to the agent’s reusable skill instructions.

Use it when a task needs repeated correction, such as fixing a failing test. Define the expected result before the run starts. Also agree how long the agent may try and when it needs help.

Define the check and every way to stop

A loop can start when a person requests it, an event occurs or a schedule runs. Each attempt needs a check of the actual result. Save progress between runs so later work can continue from the record.

Example · Improve draft saving and the skill that builds it

A coding agent adds draft saving to the service-request application using a skill: reusable instructions for planning, implementing and checking code. The team uses two connected feedback loops:

  1. Build and check the code. The agent implements saving and runs tests. The tests pass when the user edits a draft in one browser tab.
  2. Use review findings to improve the product. A reviewer tries editing the same draft in two tabs. A new test exposes a stale save overwriting newer work. The agent adds a version check so the stale save reports a conflict and retains the user’s unsaved values, then reruns the draft and regression tests.
  3. Use the failure to improve the skill. The agent proposes adding a step to identify shared resources and test simultaneous requests. The developer reviews this change to the skill instructions so future tasks include that check.
  4. Evaluate the revised skill. Run both versions on the same held-out practice tasks: tasks kept separate from the examples used to revise the skill. Use the same model version, tools, starting conditions, budget and assessment criteria. Include an unfamiliar case, such as two staff updating a request’s status. Repeat runs where outputs vary. Compare test results, review findings and the effort needed to correct the code.
  5. Keep refining from evidence. If the revised skill misses a case or causes another failure, adjust its instructions and keep that case as a regression check. Once a case informs a revision, it is no longer held out. Reserve fresh held-out tasks for the final comparison. Keep the version that meets the agreed checks without losing previously working behaviour.

The code loop corrects the draft feature. The skill loop tests whether revised instructions help on later tasks. Record both versions and their results. Passing checks ends correction and supplies evidence for review; reaching the run limit ends the attempt with unfinished work recorded.

Keep the success criteria unchanged during correction

A loop can repeat a bad assumption as well as correct a defect. Check that the tests represent the intended behaviour. Do not weaken a test merely to finish the run; review a requirements change separately.

Keep a record of what the agent tried and what each check found. Another agent may offer useful review, but can share the same mistaken assumptions.

Next step: Choose one recurring code review finding. Define a code check, propose a skill improvement and reserve held-out tasks for comparing both versions under the same conditions. Set a run limit and record the results. See how the developer workflow builds, tests and corrects a change.

Source: [7].

Graph engineering

Graph engineering means designing how work moves between agent tasks, automated checks and decision points. Each node in the graph represents an agent activity, a verification step or a routing decision. Each edge defines the condition for following that path.

Use it when a single-agent loop is not enough—for example, when specialist agents can check different properties in parallel and a routing decision determines whether to rework the code, rerun invalidated checks, pause on a blocker or advance a verified candidate.

Coordinate parallel agents and explicit decision points

A coding agent adds a CSV export to a service-request application so users can download only the records they are permitted to view. Rather than routing every finding to a person, the workflow uses an execution graph with two automated decision points and three specialist agents.

Record dependencies as well as routes. Once the coding agent produces a candidate that compiles and passes unit tests, the test, security and architecture agents run in parallel against that exact commit. A join decision waits for all three results. If any finding triggers a code change, earlier check results on the superseded commit are invalidated and rerun before the candidate can advance.

Example · Multi-agent routing while building a CSV export

The workflow graph coordinates four specialised agents and two decision gates before a developer reviews the completed change:

  • Decision 1 · Fast build gate: when the coding agent finishes a candidate, the graph runs compile and unit checks first. If a type error or broken unit test appears, the graph routes the error directly back to the coding agent without invoking the specialist agents.
  • Parallel specialist verification: once the build gate passes, the graph fans out to three agents against the same commit—the test agent checks CSV column headers and pagination streaming, the security agent verifies that queries filter out another team’s restricted records, and the architecture agent checks that the controller does not bypass the service layer.
  • Decision 2 · Join and route findings: after all three agents finish, the join node inspects their structured reports:
    • If the security agent flags a missing tenant filter or the architecture agent detects a layer violation, the router sends both structured findings back to the coding agent, marks the previous test run as stale, and reruns the graph on the revised commit.
    • If an agent encounters an unspecified rule—such as whether archived requests belong in the export—or reaches the retry cap, the router pauses the run and records a single escalation for the task owner.
    • When all three specialist agents pass on the same commit, the router bundles the diff and verification evidence into a verified candidate for merge review.

Each decision point uses explicit conditions rather than open-ended agent conversation. Humans are not pulled into intermediate syntax, test or boundary fixes; they review the verified candidate or resolve genuine specification gaps.

Keep routing rules explicit

Give each decision point a clear condition, state transition and retry bound. When a rework branch updates the code, invalidate earlier check results so the join node never combines pass notices from different commits.

A graph adds coordination work. Use a single-agent loop when a task only needs repeated test-and-fix steps. Running separate review agents catches cross-cutting defects early, but their position in the graph does not replace final human accountability for merge or release.

Next step: Map one development workflow. Mark which agent checks can run in parallel on the same commit, what condition triggers a rework loop and when the graph should pause for a person. Use the story-planning guidance and the task review and approval steps.

Sources: [8]; [9].

Software factories

In this guide, a software factory brings requirements, agent work, testing, review and release controls into a repeatable delivery workflow. The aim is to turn agreed work into changes that the team can check, release and support.

Use the idea when individual coding tasks are fast but work still waits for clarification, review or release. Improving one task does not remove the constraints elsewhere in delivery.

Choose how people review and approve changes

Addy Osmani uses “light” and “dark” factory to distinguish review arrangements. In a light factory, a person reads changes before release. In a dark factory, permitted changes can be released without that reading step. These are operating choices, not levels of maturity.

For an unattended route, agree which changes are permitted, what checks are needed, who can pause it and how to recover. Running a coding task without supervision does not itself authorise merge or release.

Example · Handle a queue of service-request fixes

The team receives a reproducible search bug, an unclear upload error and a request to let managers read every draft. The first two can become development tasks. The access change waits for a product and permissions decision.

Agents work on the agreed fixes in isolated environments. Tests and a preview help a reviewer inspect the result. Approved changes follow the team’s release process; new defects and feedback return to the work queue.

Keep understanding and recovery alongside automation

Track review waiting time, rework, defects and cost before increasing throughput. Keep design decisions available and practise diagnosis and recovery. A passing test suite does not show that people can explain or repair every change.

A preview is not a production release. Preserve the approval, monitoring and recovery controls needed for the action being taken.

Next step: Choose a small group of changes and measure where they wait. Use the automation and approval guidance, then review the release checks.

Source: [10].

AI models

An AI model is trained on data to recognise patterns and produce outputs. Depending on the model, those outputs can include text, analysis or a choice from defined options. Model selection means choosing and testing a model for a particular task.

A convincing answer to one question does not show how a model will handle other tasks. Compare models on realistic examples, including difficult cases and missing information.

Understand the labels before comparing options

The labels below describe different properties and can overlap. A small model can specialise in a domain; a large model can do so too.

Model labels and what they mean
TermMeaningExample task
Large language model (LLM)MeaningA language model with many parameters: numerical values learned during training. Used for tasks such as drafting text and explaining code.Example taskDraft acceptance criteria or explain code.
Domain-specific language modelMeaningA model trained or adapted for a subject area’s language and tasks.Example taskWork with specialist service terminology.
Small language model (SLM)MeaningA language model with fewer parameters than larger alternatives. Consider it when computing resources or local operation matter.Example taskClassify a service request.
System One, from TypeSafeMeaningTypeSafe’s name for models such as Jev that answer defined questions with choices or probabilities.Example taskSelect a request category from agreed options.

A defined output format or a confidence score does not establish that an answer is correct. The model examples and research below explain the distinctions and limits.

Example · Choose a model for a coding agent

A team compares two models for its coding agent. One evaluation task is to fix draft saving so an older browser tab cannot overwrite newer service-request changes.

The harness gives both models the same code, requirements, tools and time limit. Each model produces a code change; the team runs the same tests on both results.

Fictional results for the draft-saving fix
CheckModel A’s codeModel B’s code
A user can save and reopen an incomplete requestPassPass
A stale save preserves newer work and reports a conflictFail: newer work is overwrittenPass: conflict reported and unsaved values retained
Another user cannot read or change the draftPassPass

For this task, Model B’s change meets all three checks. The developer also reviews the code and records response time, running cost and any corrections needed.

The team repeats the comparison on other representative coding tasks, keeping separate tasks for the final evaluation. It chooses a model that meets its quality, time and cost criteria across those tasks.

Model examples and research
Four dimensions of model choice
DimensionLabelsWhat to assess
ScaleLabelsLarge or small language modelWhat to assessCapability, memory and compute needs
SpecialisationLabelsGeneral-purpose or domain-specificWhat to assessPerformance on the domain’s language and tasks
Output interfaceLabelsGenerated text or typed decisionsWhat to assessWhether the task needs writing, a choice, a score or a probability
Reasoning approachLabelsFocused judgement or deliberative reasoningWhat to assessWhether the task needs one bounded judgement or extended analysis

Large language models (LLMs)

Current model examples · checked 21 October 2026: the examples below come from the providers’ latest model line-ups. Before choosing a model, check the current catalogue and record the exact version and lifecycle status.

LLMs learn from extensive datasets and can support varied tasks through instructions and examples. Current models combine language generation with reasoning, image understanding and tool calling. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra supports complex reasoning, coding and computer use; GPT-6.1 Sol offers another option for complex coding and professional work at a lower listed cost. Both accept text and images and return text, with configurable reasoning effort. [11] [16]

Anthropic’s current examples include Claude Fable 5.1 for demanding reasoning and long-running agent tasks, and Claude Opus 5.5 for agentic coding and knowledge work. Both accept text and images, return text and use adaptive thinking with configurable effort. These capabilities support development when the harness supplies relevant context, tools and checks. [17] [18]

Read the references in two ways: model documentation explains supported inputs, tools, reasoning controls and limits; model or system cards describe the provider’s evaluations and limitations. Compare candidates on your own tasks with the same context, tools and acceptance criteria. Check the provider’s current catalogue and lifecycle guidance before choosing a version. [19]

Use and limits: consider a general-purpose LLM for varied drafting, explanation and coding work. Larger size alone does not establish quality on your task. Compare correctness, latency and cost using representative examples, including cases where evidence is missing.

Domain-specific language models

A domain-specific language model is trained or adapted for the terminology and tasks of a field, such as finance or biomedicine. Specialisation can use domain-focused training, continued pretraining or task fine-tuning. Gururangan and colleagues found benefits from continued domain and task pretraining across their classification experiments. [12]

BloombergGPT illustrates that specialisation and scale can coexist: its 50 billion parameters were trained using financial and general-purpose data. Its reported gains concern the evaluated financial tasks, not every specialist application. [13]

Use and limits: consider specialisation when domain language causes recurring errors and suitable training data exists. Compare it with a general model supplied with relevant reference material. Retrieval supplies context at use time; it does not by itself retrain the model. Here, “domain-specific” refers to a subject area, not a domain-specific programming language (DSL).

Small language models (SLMs)

SLMs use fewer parameters than larger alternatives, usually reducing model storage and memory needs. There is no single parameter threshold used consistently across model families. The Phi-3 report describes Phi-3-mini, a 3.8-billion-parameter model small enough for phone deployment, trained with carefully selected and synthetic data. [14]

Use and limits: consider an SLM for bounded tasks such as request classification or field extraction, especially when local operation matters. Measure performance on the intended hardware. Small size does not guarantee fast responses, accurate answers or private operation; deployment and data handling still matter.

System One model (System 1)

“System 1” is an analogy for fast, intuitive judgement, contrasted with slower, deliberate “System 2” reasoning. TypeSafe AI uses System One for a model class that turns application state and predefined questions into typed decisions and probabilities. Its model, Jev, supplies focused judgements that application code can combine into a workflow. This product meaning is more specific than asking an LLM to answer quickly. [21] [22]

What Jev receives and returns: its documented input is text, including strings, JSON objects and arrays of text. It evaluates questions against that state and returns constrained answers rather than writing a reply or code. The three question types are: [22] [23]

  • Choice: select from defined options, such as the team that should receive a ticket; return the choice and a probability distribution.
  • Score: assess the state against defined, ordered levels, such as an urgency rubric; return a score and probabilities across those levels.
  • Noul: estimate the probability that a statement is true, from 0 to 1, such as whether a request mentions an outage.

Questions in the same request are evaluated independently against the same state. Code combines their answers, checks permissions and decides the next action. If a later question needs an earlier answer, build a follow-up request with that result. Open-ended writing and complex reasoning can remain with a generative model or a person. [23]

Confidence needs interpretation: Choice and Score include a confidence statistic derived from their probability distributions. Noul returns a yes/no probability without a separate confidence field. Confidence is not proof of correctness, and a valid output type does not establish that the judgement is right. Check accuracy and calibration on representative, held-out cases before setting thresholds for action, further analysis or human review. [24]

What the evidence supports: TypeSafe reports speed and cost gains on its own workflows; those gains depend on the comparison and deployment conditions. A separate 2026 preprint, Fast Models, Slow Evidence, found Jev stronger than the compared model on many decision points, but both performed at chance on its zero-shot model-routing task. It also showed how omitted costs and thresholds fitted on evaluation data could overstate deployment benefits. This is early, task-specific evidence rather than a general guarantee. [21] [25]

Example · Triage a service request with Jev

Supply a request’s text, relevant service details and the triage rubric. Ask separately for its category, urgency and whether it reports an outage. Application code applies the validated routing rules. Uncertain, conflicting or uncovered cases go to a person; an LLM can draft a response when needed. Keep access and release approvals in their existing decision process.

Related research: Yu and colleagues’ System 2 distillation work concerns training models to answer directly from reasoning-derived examples. GPT-6 Astra reasoning effort and Claude thinking controls vary deliberation within generative models. These are related ways to balance computation and quality, but they do not establish the typed-decision interface that defines Jev. [15] [20] [17] [18]

Evaluate the complete task

Use the information, tools and permissions that the model will actually receive. Compare results with the current approach, including rules or human handling where relevant. A smaller model does not guarantee speed or privacy, and a larger one does not guarantee better results.

Next step: Choose one task and agree its acceptance criteria before comparing models. Use the testing and independent review guidance, and retain cases where a model fails for future checks.

Sources and learning references

The references provide further explanation and examples for each practice.

Learning references

Use these courses, guides and playbooks for detailed instruction and practice. Check the implementation courses for prerequisites and tool requirements.

  • Intent-driven development: CircleCI’s guide explains how to carry outcomes, constraints and success criteria through a change.
  • Spec-driven development: AI Agent Factory crash course covers specifications, planning and implementation tasks.
  • Context engineering: Context engineering resource collection gathers techniques, research and a learning roadmap. Read the intent-driven.dev overview for the concept’s role in defining requirements.
  • Harness engineering: Walking Labs provides explanations, projects and templates. The AI Agent Factory crash course adds practice with controls and verification.
  • Loop engineering: Iwo Szapar’s playbook provides a design canvas. The AI Agent Factory crash course covers triggers, saved progress and checks.
  • Graph engineering: AI Agent Factory crash course develops parallel branches, checking and merging.
  • Software factory: Vercel Academy provides an implementation course. Addy Osmani’s article discusses review arrangements and the limits of autonomy.
  • Models: explore GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 for current examples of reasoning and tool-supported work, checked on 21 October 2026. Read the GPT-6 model guide for reasoning controls and the matching Claude model or system card for provider evaluations. Check the current catalogue and record the exact version and lifecycle status before choosing a model. Use domain adaptation research, BloombergGPT, the Phi-3 report and System 2 distillation research for the underlying concepts.
  • System One and Jev: read TypeSafe’s System One explanation, question primitives and confidence guidance, then compare its provider claims with the separate evaluation preprint. Start with one bounded decision and measure it against your current approach.
